props.title: That Obscure Object of Desire

sections.content: Luis Buñuel's final masterpiece That Obscure Object of Desire brilliantly employs two actresses (Carole Bouquet and Angela Molina) to play the same character, Conchita, without ever acknowledging the switch. This surrealist technique amplifies the film's exploration of frustrated desire and impossible love. Like Buñuel's earlier Belle de Jour (1967) and The Discreet Charm of the Bourgeoisie (1972), it mercilessly satirizes bourgeois society while diving deep into psychological obsession.

sections.content: The film's influence echoes through later works exploring romantic obsession and fractured identity. Vertigo (1958) shares its themes of impossible romantic idealization, while Persona (1966) similarly plays with dual female identities. The technique of using multiple actors for one role later appears in I'm Not There (2007), where six actors portray Bob Dylan, and Holy Motors (2012), which features multiple identity shifts.

Buñuel's mastery of surrealist cinema reaches its apex here, blending political commentary with psychological insight. The recurring terrorist attacks in the background serve as both social commentary and metaphor for explosive desire, while the mysterious sack Mathieu carries becomes an absurdist symbol of emotional baggage. This approach influenced directors like David Lynch, particularly in Mulholland Drive (2001) and Lost Highway (1997). SUBHEAD: The Legacy of Surrealist Cinema

sections.content: The film's innovative narrative structure and dreamlike logic created a template for modern surrealist cinema. Directors like Charlie Kaufman with Synecdoche, New York (2008) and Yorgos Lanthimos with The Lobster (2015) carry forward Buñuel's tradition of using absurdist elements to explore deep psychological truths. The film's examination of class structures and social hypocrisy remains startlingly relevant.
